sections.title: Build your introduction from four lines
body: Copy whole chunks before studying grammar: Jag heter … · Jag bor i … · Jag kommer från … · Jag talar … Say Jag heter Alex. Mitt namn är Alex is correct too, but it sounds like filling in a form.

The slip beginners make most: mixing two boxes. Jag bor i tells where you live now. Jag kommer från tells where you come from. Join them with men (but): Jag kommer från Indien, men jag bor i Helsingfors nu.

The first sound of every chunk: Swedish J is always the y in yes (Hindi य), never the j in jam (ज). Jag sounds like yaag, ja like yaa. Hindi written in English letters uses j for ज (jaldi), so this slip comes easily.

In Swedish, use the Swedish names of places in Finland: Helsingfors (Helsinki), Esbo (Espoo), Vanda (Vantaa), Åbo (Turku). Helsingfors is stressed at the end: hel-sing-FORS. The Finnish name HEL-sin-ki pulls you to the start.

Use och before the last language, with no comma before och (English often puts one there). Put lite directly before each language you speak only a little, as your teacher did: Jag talar engelska, svenska, lite ryska och lite portugisiska. Language names take a small letter: hindi, svenska.

sections.title: Nine vowels: copy the mouth first
body: The Swedish alphabet is the English one plus three letters at the end: å, ä, ö (29 letters; a dictionary lists them after z). Swedish has nine vowel letters: A, O, U, Y, I, E, Ö, Ä, Å. First copy the lip and tongue position; then copy the audio.
English, Hindi, and Marathi examples are memory bridges, not exact Swedish pronunciation. The Swedish recording is the final model.

Two surprises for a Hindi speaker: Swedish O usually sounds close to ऊ (bok, bor), and the ओ sound you know is usually written Å (från, hår). U, Y and Ö have no Hindi or Marathi match. If you have heard Finnish around Helsinki, Finnish y, ö and ä are close to the Swedish ones.
Rounded lips: O, U, Y, Ö, Å. Front tongue: I, E, Y, Ä, Ö. Notice that Y and Ö belong to both groups.

activity.label: Mouth map

features.label: Rounded lips
features.note: O, U, Y, Ö and Å push the lips forward into a circle. Check in a mirror.

features.label: Front vowels
features.note: E, I, Y, Ä and Ö keep the tongue forward. Remember this group: it softens g, k and sk in topic 4.

sounds.cue: Open wide and let the sound sit at the back of the mouth. आ is a starting bridge.
Round the lips as in boots. In these words Swedish O sounds close to a long oo or ऊ, with tighter lips.
Tight rounded lips, as if drinking through a straw. Long u in du and short u in dum sound different: copy each one.
Say I, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for U.
Wide smile, tongue high and forward. ई is a starting bridge.
A lighter smile than I. ए is a starting bridge.
Say E, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for O.
Drop the jaw as for A, but aim for E. Near Hindi ऐ in है (not the Marathi ai). Before r, as in bär, it opens even more.
The real O: deep and round. Long å, as in från and hår, is near Hindi ओ. A short å, as in och, is more open, near ऑ.

contrasts.cue: Same trick: keep the E tongue, round the lips.

contrasts.cue: Swedish O often sounds like oo (ऊ). The O you know from Hindi ओ is usually written Å.

sections.title: Long or short: stretch one part
body: Stress first: most Swedish words are stressed on the first syllable (SVEN-ska, MAM-ma, IN-di-en). Loanwords often keep a late stress (ka-FÉ, pa-ra-PLY), and so does your city: hel-sing-FORS. Stress and length help people understand you more than a perfect vowel does.
In a stressed Swedish syllable, either the vowel is long or the consonant after it is long. Hear both parts, not only the vowel.

A common spelling clue is: one consonant letter after the stressed vowel often means a longer vowel; a doubled consonant often means a short vowel and longer consonant. Your teacher's English bridge works the same way: write (long i) and written (short i before tt). It is a clue, not a rule without exceptions.
Use the routine: find the stressed vowel → look right → listen → copy the whole word.

sections.title: One vowel group, three soft sounds
body: The spelling group E, I, Y, Ä, Ö often softens the consonant immediately before it. These are front vowels because the tongue is forward; Y and Ö still use rounded lips. The softening happens mainly at the start of a word or a stressed syllable; later in a word the consonant often stays hard, as the k in pojke (boy).
G usually becomes the Swedish j sound, K usually becomes the tj sound /ɕ/, and SK usually becomes the sj sound /ɧ/ before this group.

Two accents, both correct. In Finland-Swedish, the Swedish you hear in Helsinki, tj sounds close to ch in chai (your teacher's ciao) and sj sounds close to English sh (श). The app's voices are from Sweden: their tj is a soft hiss with no t, and their sj is a breathier, rounder sound. Copy whichever you hear around you; people understand both.
Use the shortcut to predict, then use audio to learn the actual sound. Some loanwords are exceptions. One habit to avoid: do not put an i before sk, as in iskärm. Say skärm, ska, skuld straight away.

activity.summary: One question does most of the work: which vowel comes next? Front vowels (e, i, y, ä, ö) soften g, k and sk into three different sounds; back vowels leave them hard. Sj, skj and tj keep their sound whatever follows. Some loanwords break the rule, so trust the recording.

sections.title: Recognise the remaining Lesson 1 spellings
body: Recognition only today: SJ and SKJ normally use the sj sound, as in sjuk and skjorta. At the start of a word, HJ, DJ and LJ are said as the Swedish j alone: hjälp sounds like yelp, djur like yoor, ljus like yoos.

RS is where the two accents differ. In Sweden the r melts into the s, giving a sh made with the tongue tip curled back, as for Hindi ट or ड. That is your teacher's sh in kurs and mars. Finland-Swedish usually keeps R + S separate, so in Helsinki you hear hel-sing-FORS, while the app's Sweden voices say something closer to hel-sing-FOSH. Both are correct.

Plain Swedish t and d are dental, like Hindi त and द: the tongue touches the back of the top teeth. Say tack with त, not with the ट that Indian English often uses for t. Good news for Helsinki: Finland-Swedish says t and k without a puff of air, like your plain त and क, and rolls or taps r much like Hindi र. The app's Sweden voices add a small puff of air after t and k, and their r is softer.
Och is /ɔk/ in careful speech and often just å in conversation.

examples.en: sick · shirt
examples.note: Two spellings for the sj sound.

examples.en: help · light
examples.note: Initial H or L is silent in these spellings; begin with Swedish j.

examples.note: Sweden: one curled-tongue sh. Finland-Swedish: r + s kept apart. Choose one and be consistent.

guided.prompt: Jag, ja, hej: which Hindi letter matches the Swedish j?

guided.explanation: Swedish j is always य: jag sounds like yaag, ja like yaa. The ज sound of English jam is not what the letter j means in Swedish.

guided.prompt: Jag bor i Helsingfors. Where is the stress in Helsingfors?

guided.explanation: Helsingfors is stressed at the end, in Finland and in Sweden. Most Swedish words are stressed at the start, and the Finnish HEL-sin-ki is too, so this one needs practice.

guided.prompt: Which row maps the three common soft sounds correctly?
answers: gillar → j; kött → tj; skärm → sj
options: gillar → j; kött → tj; skärm → sj
gillar → sj; kött → j; skärm → tj
gillar → hard g; kött → hard k; skärm → hard sk
guided.hint: The front vowels are i in gillar, ö in kött, and ä in skärm.
guided.explanation: Before a front vowel, g, k, and sk usually become three different soft sounds: j, tj, and sj.

checkpoint.prompt: Elin has told you where she comes from. Now ask her in Swedish: ‘Which languages do you speak?’
checkpoint.hint: Question word first, then the verb, then du. Elin asks Alex the same thing in the dialogue.
checkpoint.explanation: Vilka språk talar du? Vilka = which (for more than one). The verb talar comes straight after the question words, before du.

checkpoint.prompt: New words, same rule. Which word starts with the tj sound?
checkpoint.hint: Look at the vowel right after the first consonant. Is it e, i, y, ä or ö?
checkpoint.explanation: K + ö, a soft vowel, gives the tj sound: kör. In kan and god a hard vowel follows, so k and g stay hard.

checkpoint.prompt: New words, same clue. Which one has a long, stretched vowel?
checkpoint.hint: Look right after the stressed vowel: one consonant letter or two?
checkpoint.explanation: Hus has one s, so the u is long. Buss and kaffe have a double consonant, so the vowel is short, just like tak and tack.

assignment.title: Episode 1 mission: Say who you are
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Say your real four-line introduction once slowly and once at normal speed: name, home now, origin, and languages.

ONE SOUND LOOP: Choose only one: tak/tack OR gillar/kött/skärm. Listen and repeat the small set three times.

RETURN: Close the model and give your real introduction from memory in under 20 seconds.
assignment.model:
Hej! Jag heter Alex.
Jag bor i Helsingfors.
Jag kommer från Indien.
Jag talar hindi, engelska och lite svenska.

takeaways: Core: say Jag heter … · Jag bor i … · Jag kommer från … · Jag talar … as four complete chunks.
Two boxes: bor i = home now, kommer från = origin. Join them with men: … men jag bor i Helsingfors nu.
Swedish j is always य, the y in yes: jag = yaag. Stress your city at the end: hel-sing-FORS.
Mouth first, audio second: use the Hindi/Marathi/English bridge to find the shape, then copy the Swedish model.
Practise one contrast at a time: tak/tack or the g → j, k → tj, sk → sj pattern.
Two accents, both correct: in Helsinki tj sounds like ch and sj like sh; the app's Sweden voices say them more softly.

points: Greet the class and say your name.

sections.title: Greet: choose the right question
body: In Finland, Hej is the everyday greeting everywhere: in shops, at work, and with friends. Finland-Swedish speakers often say Hej hej, and in southern Finland you will also hear the informal Morjens.
The everyday check-in is Hur är det? or Hur är det med dig? (How are things with you?). Very casual friends say Läget? or Hur är läget? (What's up?).
Hur mår du? asks more personally how someone feels. Friends use it too, and it is the natural question when someone has been ill or tired: Mår du bättre nu?

examples.fi: Hej! Hur är det med dig?
examples.en: Hi! How are things with you?
examples.note: A safe everyday check-in with anyone.

examples.fi: Hej hej! Hur är det?
examples.en: Hi! How's it going?
examples.note: Hej hej is very common in Finland-Swedish, as a greeting and as goodbye.

examples.fi: Morjens! Läget?
examples.en: Hey! What's up?
examples.note: Very casual. Recognise it; use it with friends.

examples.fi: Hur mår du? Mår du bättre nu?
examples.en: How are you feeling? Are you feeling better now?
examples.note: A real question about how someone feels.

rows: Hur är det? · Hur är det med dig?
friends, or when someone has been ill
Hej with anyone; Morjens with friends

sections.memoryTip: Everyday: Hur är det? Personal: Hur mår du? Casual: Läget? When in doubt in Finland, Hej! and Hur är det? always work.

sections.title: How are you? Pick an honest answer
body: Whichever question you hear, a short answer is enough: Bra, tack. Och du? You do not need to tell your whole day to someone you barely know.
Answer with the verb you hear: Hur är det? → Det är bra. Hur mår du? → Jag mår bra. You will also hear Jag är bra in casual speech, and Bara bra (just fine).
Then send the question back with Och du?, the same move you learned in Lecture 1. Stress du: och DU? The stress shows that you are turning the question around.

examples.fi: Hur är det? — Det är bra, tack.
examples.en: How's it going? — It's good, thanks.
examples.note: är det → det är: the answer mirrors the question.

examples.fi: Bara bra, tack! Och du?
examples.en: Just fine, thanks! And you?
examples.note: Bara bra is a very common short answer.

examples.fi: Jättebra!
examples.en: Really good!
examples.note: Jätte- makes it stronger. It works in any situation.

examples.fi: Hur mår du? — Jag mår toppen!

examples.note: Lite from Lecture 1 makes it softer.

examples.en: I feel pretty bad.

sections.title: Pronouns: point to people without names
body: Swedish subject pronouns: jag (I), du (you, one person), han (he), hon (she), hen (they, one person), vi (we), ni (you, two or more), de (they).
Good news: the verb is the same for every person. Jag bor, du bor, han bor, vi bor, de bor. English adds -s (he lives) and Hindi changes the ending (रहता, रहती, रहते); Swedish never does.

English has one word, you. Swedish counts the people: du is singular (one person), ni is plural (two or more). Swedish has no polite you like Hindi आप or Marathi तुम्ही, so say du to one person, even a teacher, a doctor or a shop assistant. In Finland you may hear ni to one older stranger as extra politeness, but du is the normal choice.

Hen means one person without saying he or she, like English singular they. Use it when you do not know or it does not matter (En ny elev kommer. Hen heter Kim.), and for people who are neither he nor she. It works like Finnish hän. De (they, two or more) is written de but said dom.
Things are not han or hon. A thing is den or det (it): on page 6 the milk is den (Den är slut).
A common trap: someone and I together is vi (we). Alex says: Rohan och jag kommer från Pune. Vi talar hindi. When you talk to two people, use ni: Hej Priya och Rohan! Talar ni engelska?

sections.title: People in your life: family and relationships
body: Family words are nouns: syster, bror, barn. Build sentences with the verbs har (have) and är (am, is, are): Jag har en syster. Jag är gift.

Swedish glues words together into compound words: pojke + vän = pojkvän (boyfriend), flicka + vän = flickvän (girlfriend). Bo means live, as in Jag bor i: a sambo lives together with a partner, a särbo lives apart.

Useful status words: gift (married), sambo, singel, skild (divorced; skilja sig = to get divorced), and Jag bor ensam (I live alone). After är, a status word needs no en: Jag är gift. Jag är sambo. After har, a person gets en: Jag har en sambo. Jag har en syster. Barn means child or children; syskon means brothers and sisters together.

examples.fi: Jag har en syster och en bror.
examples.en: I have a sister and a brother.
examples.note: En before one person: en syster, en bror.

examples.fi: Jag är sambo. Han heter Mikko.
examples.en: I live with my partner. His name is Mikko.
examples.note: Sambo: partners who live together without being married. Very common in Finland and Sweden.

examples.en: I'm married. I have a wife.
examples.note: Man = husband, fru = wife. Make and maka are formal words for spouse.

examples.fi: Jag är singel och jag bor ensam.
examples.en: I'm single and I live alone.

examples.fi: De har två barn, en son och en dotter.
examples.en: They have two children, a son and a daughter.
examples.note: Barn is both child and children. One child is ett barn, not en barn (en and ett come in a later lesson).

sections.title: Question words: ask the next question
body: Vad = what, hur = how, var = where, varifrån = where from, när = when, varför = why, vem = who.

Word order: question word → verb → subject (the person). Var bor du? När kommer de? The verb comes second. If the question part is two words, like hur gammal, the verb comes right after both: Hur gammal är du?

English adds do: Where do you live? Swedish has no do. Var bor du? is word for word 'where live you'. Hindi puts the verb last (तुम कहाँ रहते हो?), but Swedish moves it up to second place. So never Var du bor?
A yes/no question starts with the verb itself: Är du gift? Har du syskon? Talar du svenska? You met Vilka språk talar du? in Lecture 1; vilken, vilket and vilka (which) come back in a later lesson.

examples.en: What are you buying?

sections.title: Hear it the way people say it
body: Written and spoken Swedish differ a little. Recognise these short forms now, and keep writing the full forms.
De is said dom. Jag is often just ja. Är often shrinks to e, det to de, and vad to va. In Finland you will also hear de said as it is written.
So Hur är det? often sounds like hur e de?, and De mår bra sounds like dom mår bra.
Length from Lecture 1 still decides the sound: one consonant after the stressed vowel usually means stretch it (mår, hur, när); two mean stop it (trött, toppen, syster).

Today's small words break that clue: han, hon, den, vem, man and vän have a short vowel, although only one n or m follows. Short words like these are spelled with one n or m at the end. The o in hon sounds like the oo in English book.

assignment.instructions:
CORE: Answer Hur mår du? honestly and send it back with Och du? Then present two people in your life: who they are (Det är min …), their name (Hon heter … / Han heter …), and where they live.

QUESTION LOOP: Ask three questions with different question words, for example Var bor du? När kommer du? Varför pluggar du svenska? Keep the verb second.

RETURN: Without looking, say how you are and introduce one person in under 20 seconds.
assignment.model:
Jag mår bra, tack. Och du?
Det är min syster. Hon heter Priya. Hon bor i Indien.
Det är min vän. Hon heter Elin. Hon är sambo och hon bor i Helsingfors.
Var bor du? När kommer du? Varför pluggar du svenska?

takeaways: Greet with Hej and Hur är det?, keep Hur mår du? for how someone really feels, then answer short and ask back: Bra, tack. Och DU?
Pronouns: jag, du, han, hon, hen, vi, ni, de, and the verb stays the same for all of them. Count the people for du and ni; write de but say dom.
Question word → verb → person: Var bor du? När kommer de? Never Var du bor?

hunt.label: Verb-form hunt
hunt.title: Find the present, command and infinitive forms.
hunt.instructions: This page does not colour its verbs, but its note card says infinitiv och imperativ. Tap each verb form below and see which job it does.
hunt.missHint: Look at kommer, kom and komma, at grillar and grilla, and at sitt, sitta and sitter.

spots.rule: Present tense, ends in r: När kommer du hem? = When are you coming home?
Command: kommer loses er and keeps one m. Kom snabbt! = Come quickly!
Infinitive after the help verb måste: måste komma.
Present tense, ends in r: Jag grillar = I am grilling.
Infinitive after kan: kan inte grilla. For ar verbs it looks just like the command (Grilla!).
Command: sitter loses er. Sitt! = Sit!
Infinitive after kan: Kan du sitta? A polite way to ask.
Present tense: Hunden sitter = the dog sits.

Both spellings are correct. Språkrådet recommends the two-word i morgon, and this app uses it in its own lines. Morgon alone means morning.

hunt.label: Help-verb and inte hunt
hunt.title: Find inte and the four help verbs the page marks.
hunt.instructions: On the page, inte is red and the help verbs kan, vill, måste and ska are in italics. Tap each one and see what follows it.
hunt.missHint: Look for the red inte, and for the italic word just before an infinitive: kan, vill, måste, ska.

spots.rule: Inte (not) comes straight after the first verb: kan inte, vill inte, vet inte. In the command Oroa dig inte, it comes after oroa dig.
Kan (can) is a help verb. The next verb is an infinitive: kan läsa, kan sova. Kan du …? asks for help politely.
Vill (want to) is a help verb: vill sova.
Måste (must, have to) is a help verb: måste klara, måste sova, måste jobba.
Ska is a help verb too: vad jag ska göra = what I should do.

sections.title: Three verb forms: now, command, dictionary
body: A verb is a doing word. Today you need three verb forms. The present tense says what happens now or regularly. It ends in r: talar, köper, bor. The help verbs kan, vill, ska and måste are the exceptions, and so is vet (know) on page 8: Jag vet inte. Swedish uses one form for I study and I am studying: Jag pluggar. English (I am studying) and Hindi (मैं पढ़ रहा हूँ, main padh rahā hūn) both add am. Swedish never does, so Jag är pluggar is wrong.

The imperative (command form) tells someone to do something: Tala! Köp! Ring! Your teacher calls it the naked verb. Later tenses are built on it, so it is worth learning well. The infinitive is the dictionary form. It follows a help verb and usually ends in a: tala, köpa, ringa. Dictionaries often show it with att (to): att tala = to speak.

Make the forms from the present tense, in three groups. Ar verbs: take away r. Talar becomes Tala! and tala; the command and the infinitive look the same. Er verbs: take away er for the command, then add a for the infinitive. Köper becomes Köp! and köpa. Short verbs: take away r. Bor becomes Bo! and bo; this infinitive does not end in a (also må).

Two verbs need extra care. Vara (be) is irregular: är in the present and Var! as a command. Kommer keeps only one m in the command: Kom! The infinitive is komma. The o in Kom! stays short, as in kommer: Swedish never writes mm at the end of a word. So Kom hem! has two short vowels (remember long and short from Lecture 1).

activity.label: Sort verb forms

activity.instructions: Look only at the Swedish: an r ending, a help verb before it, or no subject at all. Is the marked verb the present, a command, or the infinitive?

items.fi: Jag köper bröd.
items.why: Köper ends in r: present tense. Jag köper bröd = I buy bread.

items.fi: Köp bröd!

items.fi: Jag vill köpa bröd.
items.why: After vill, the verb ends in a: köpa. Jag vill köpa bröd = I want to buy bread.

items.fi: Ring mig!
items.why: Ringer loses er: Ring! is the command. Ring mig! = Call me!

items.fi: Hon måste ringa nu.
items.why: After måste, use the infinitive ringa. Hon måste ringa nu = She must call now.

items.fi: Var glad!
items.why: Var! is the command of vara (be). Var glad! = Be happy!

activity.summary: Ask what the verb is doing: telling what happens (present, r), giving an instruction (command), or following a help verb (infinitive).

sections.title: Help verbs open the door to an infinitive
body: Kan (can), vill (want to), måste (must, have to) and ska (will, be going to) are help verbs. The verb after them is the infinitive, with no att: kan tala, vill köpa, måste jobba, ska träna. Not kan talar, and not vill att köpa, even though English says want to. On page 8, Jag vill inte att du blir sen has att only because a new person (du) does the second action.
Careful with vill. It looks like English will, but it means want to. For a plan (will, going to), use ska: I morgon ska jag träna.
Hinner (have time to) and orkar (have the energy to) work the same way: Jag hinner gå till affären. Jag orkar inte plugga. After these two, att is possible but never needed.

Two useful questions. Kan du …? asks for help politely: Kan du hjälpa mig? Ska vi …? suggests a plan: Ska vi dricka kaffe? To want a thing, say vill ha: Jag vill ha kaffe, not Jag vill kaffe. In a café, order with tack: En kaffe, tack. Snälla at the start of a sentence sounds like begging.

Careful: English must not is not måste inte in Swedish. A ban is får inte: Du får inte röka här (You must not smoke here). No need is behöver inte: Du behöver inte komma (You don’t have to come). Lecture 13 practises both.

examples.fi: Jag kan sjunga, men jag kan inte dansa.
examples.en: I can sing, but I cannot dance.
examples.note: Both verbs after kan are infinitives.

examples.fi: Jag vill ha kaffe.
examples.en: I want coffee.
examples.note: Use vill ha for wanting a thing.

examples.fi: I morgon ska jag träffa Elin.
examples.en: Tomorrow I’m going to meet Elin.

examples.fi: Jag måste ringa hälsostationen.
examples.en: I have to call the health centre.
examples.note: In Helsinki the public health centre is called hälsostation in Swedish (in Sweden: vårdcentral).

examples.fi: Jag hinner gå till affären.
examples.en: I have time to go to the shop.

examples.fi: Kan du hjälpa mig?
examples.en: Can you help me?
examples.note: Kan du …? is a polite request.

examples.en: Shall we have coffee?

A wish: you would like to

Orkar is about energy. Jag orkar inte = I am too tired.

activity.pattern: Help verb + infinitive: kan simma, vill sova, måste jobba, ska träna.

sections.title: Inte comes after the first verb
body: Inte means not. It makes a sentence negative. Put inte straight after the first verb. One verb: Jag simmar inte. With a help verb: Jag kan inte simma. Kan is the first verb, so inte comes before the infinitive simma.

English adds do: I do not swim. Swedish never adds an extra verb. The rule works with every help verb: Jag vill inte ha kaffe. Jag hinner inte komma. In a command, inte also follows the verb: Läs inte mer! Oroa dig inte!

If you think in Hindi, watch out. Hindi puts नहीं before the verb (मैं नहीं जाता, main nahīn jātā = I don’t go), so Jag inte går may feel right. Swedish wants Jag går inte. Marathi puts नाही after the verb (मी जात नाही, mī jāt nāhī), which is closer to Swedish. But Marathi नाही ends the sentence, and Swedish inte does not: Jag talar inte finska, not Jag talar finska inte.
Short adverbs such as ofta (often), alltid (always) and aldrig (never) go in the same place as inte: Jag dricker ofta kaffe. Jag dricker aldrig vin.
Finland-Swedish note: in fast speech in Helsinki you will often hear int instead of inte. Recognise it, but write inte.

sections.title: The verb stays second
body: The golden rule of Swedish word order is verb second (V2): in a statement, the first verb is always the second building block. Position one can be the person (Min mamma bakar en kaka i dag), a time (I dag bakar min mamma en kaka) or a place (I Finland dricker vi mycket kaffe).

The subject always stands right next to the verb: just before it or just after it. When a time or a place comes first, the subject moves to just after the verb. Count chunks, not words: I dag is one chunk in position one.

With a help verb and inte: I morgon ska jag inte jobba. Ska is in position two, then jag, then inte, then the infinitive (verb 2) in its own slot. Questions with a question word follow the same rule: Varför kommer du sent?

Two common slips. English says Today I work, so learners say I dag jag jobbar. Swedish needs I dag jobbar jag. Hindi and Marathi put the verb near the end, so check that the verb has not drifted to the end. Learners of Swedish often master this swap late, so say time-first lines aloud many times.

examples.fi: Min mamma bakar en kaka i dag.
examples.en: My mother is baking a cake today.

examples.fi: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.
examples.en: Today my mother is baking a cake.
examples.note: Time first, then the verb, then the subject.

examples.fi: Tyvärr kan jag inte komma i kväll.
examples.en: Unfortunately I can’t come tonight.
examples.note: Tyvärr (unfortunately) is position one, so kan comes next. Later in the sentence it goes where inte goes: Jag kan tyvärr inte komma.

examples.fi: I Finland dricker vi mycket kaffe varje dag.
examples.en: In Finland we drink a lot of coffee every day.

examples.fi: Varför kommer du sent?
examples.en: Why are you late?
examples.note: The question word is position one; kommer is position two.

sections.memoryTip: Start with who, when or where. Then the verb must arrive immediately.

guided.prompt: Jag kan ___ svenska.

guided.explanation: Kan tala: after a help verb, use the infinitive, without att (English to does not carry over).

guided.prompt: Alex says: “Jag är så trött!” Choose the right verb (sover, köper, ringer), then type its command form: ___ nu!
guided.hint: A tired person needs sleep. Sover is an er verb: take away er.
guided.explanation: Sov nu! Sover loses er: Sov! Elin says the same thing in the story.

guided.prompt: Choose the correct Swedish for “I am studying.”
guided.hint: Swedish present covers both study and am studying.
guided.explanation: Jag pluggar. English I am studying and Hindi पढ़ रहा हूँ both have am; Swedish has no am here.

guided.prompt: There is no help verb here. Elin ___ kaffe varje morgon.
guided.hint: Without kan, vill, måste or ska, use the present tense.
guided.explanation: Elin dricker kaffe varje morgon. With no help verb, the verb is in the present (r). Compare: Elin vill dricka kaffe.

guided.prompt: Alex’s test is tomorrow. He says: “I have to study tonight.” Jag ___ plugga i kväll.
guided.hint: Have to is a need, not a wish or an ability.
guided.explanation: Jag måste plugga i kväll. Måste = must, have to.

guided.prompt: Make a softer request: “Can you speak slowly, please?” ___ du tala långsamt, snälla?
guided.hint: Ask about ability to make it polite.
guided.explanation: Kan du …? is a polite request. Måste du …? means Do you have to …?

guided.prompt: Make it negative and type the whole sentence: Jag orkar plugga. (I have the energy to study.)
guided.hint: Find the first verb, then put inte right after it.
guided.explanation: Jag orkar inte plugga: inte comes right after orkar, the first verb.

guided.prompt: Lecture 1 line: Jag bor i Finland nu. Start it with Nu (now) and type the whole sentence.
guided.hint: Nu first, then the verb, then jag.
guided.explanation: Nu bor jag i Finland. From Lecture 1: Nu takes position one, so bor stays second and jag moves after it, just like I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.

guided.prompt: A mother phones her son and says: “Come home!” Type the command of kommer with hem (home).
guided.hint: Kommer loses er, and mm becomes one m. Hem means home (page 7: När kommer du hem?).
guided.explanation: Kom hem! Kommer → Kom!, with one m.

missionPlan.intro: Elin asks: Vad kan du göra? Vad vill du göra? Vad måste du göra? Vad hinner du inte göra i veckan? Plan one line for each answer, and three for kan.

pronunciation.text: Jag kan tala. Kan du komma? Kom hem! Jag måste sova. Sov nu! Oroa dig inte!
pronunciation.tip: Long or short, as in Lecture 1. Kan has a short a (one n, like han and men), but tala has a long a. Kom! and hem are short too: Swedish never ends a word with mm. Sova and Sov! sound like ‘såva’ and ‘såv’. The app’s Sweden-Swedish voices sing two-syllable words such as tala and sova with a two-peaked melody. Finland-Swedish has no such melody, so you do not need it: just stress the first syllable. Say mig and dig like mej and dej.

writing.prompt: Write a short message: say sorry, say why you cannot meet tonight, and suggest what, where and when instead.
writing.situation: Your friend Elin writes: “Vi ses i kväll!” (See you tonight!) But you are tired and have a test tomorrow. Write back and cancel. This is a real YKI basic-level task type: a short message that cancels a plan.
points: Greet Elin.
Say sorry and say that you cannot meet tonight.
Say why: you are tired and must study.
Suggest another plan: what, where and when.
End with a greeting and your name.
writing.help: Hej Elin! · Förlåt! (Sorry!) · Tyvärr kan jag inte … (Unfortunately I can’t …: tyvärr first, then kan) · Jag är trött och måste plugga. · Vi kan dricka kaffe i centrum på fredag. (We can have coffee in the centre on Friday.) · Hinner du då? (Do you have time then?) · Hälsningar (Best wishes) and your name.
writing.model:
Hej Elin!
Förlåt! Tyvärr kan jag inte träffa dig i kväll. Jag är trött och måste plugga. I morgon har jag ett prov. Vi kan dricka kaffe i centrum på fredag. Hinner du då?
Hälsningar, Alex

route.expectedOutput: Answer Elin’s four questions about your week: three things you can do, one thing you want to do, one thing you must do, and one thing you have no time for. Then write a message: say sorry, say why you cannot meet tonight, and suggest what, where and when instead.
route.transferPrompt: Say the same plan again, but begin two lines with I dag or I morgon.
route.returnPrompt: From memory, say one kan line, one måste line and one negative line in under 20 seconds.
successChecks: Say six lines: three with kan, one with vill, one with måste and one with inte.
Use the infinitive after each help verb: kan tala, not kan talar.
Put inte after the first verb.

assignment.title: Episode 3 mission: My week
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Answer Vad kan du göra? (three things), Vad vill du göra?, Vad måste du göra? and Vad hinner du inte göra i veckan?

CHANGE: Start two lines with I dag or I morgon and keep the verb second.

RETURN: Tomorrow, say a kan line, a måste line and a negative line without looking.
assignment.model: Jag kan tala hindi och engelska. Jag kan laga mat. Jag kan simma. Jag vill träna. I morgon måste jag plugga svenska. Jag hinner inte simma i veckan.

takeaways: Present tense usually ends in r; the command is the naked verb; the infinitive is the dictionary form that follows a help verb.
After kan, vill, måste and ska, use the infinitive with no att: Jag kan tala. Jag vill sova.
Put inte after the first verb: Jag kan inte komma. In a command too: Oroa dig inte!
A time phrase may come first, but the verb stays second: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.

sections.title: En or ett: every thing has a partner
body: Every Swedish noun belongs to one of two groups: en words and ett words. This is called noun gender. En and ett are articles: both mean a or an. En dator is a computer; ett jobb is a job. The group matters later too: it decides the word for “the” and the ending of describing words (Lecture 5).

The word itself rarely shows its group, so learn the article together with the noun. Most nouns, roughly 75–80%, are en words, so en is the better guess when you are not sure. Words for people are usually en words: en kvinna, en läkare. A useful exception is ett barn (a child).

Some endings give a clue. Nouns that end in -a are nearly always en words: en lista, en vecka (exceptions: ett öga, an eye; ett hjärta, a heart). Nouns that end in -are, -ing or -het are en words too: en lärare, en tidning (a newspaper), en frihet (freedom). Nouns that end in -um are ett words: ett museum, ett gymnasium.

A compound word is two words joined into one. The last part decides the gender. Dator is an en word, but spel is an ett word, so datorspel is an ett word: ett datorspel. Lista is an en word, so önskelista is too: en önskelista.

Hindi and Marathi give nouns a gender too, but en and ett are not male and female: en pojke (a boy) and en flicka (a girl) are both en words. They also have no articles (no a or the), so it is easy to leave en or ett out. Say it each time you name one thing: Det är en dator, not Det är dator. (A few fixed phrases have none: söker jobb, spelar piano.)

sections.title: Work: what you do and where
body: Ask Vad jobbar du med? (What do you do for work?). The answer usually uses jobbar som plus the job: Jag jobbar som lärare. Do not put en or ett before the job, not even after är: Jag är lärare. English says a teacher, so Jag är en lärare is the classic slip. (With a describing word, en comes back: en bra lärare.) Jobbar already means work or am working, so never say Jag är jobbar, just as Jag pluggar in Lecture 3.

Use jobbar på plus the workplace. The workplace keeps its article: på en skola, på ett sjukhus, på ett kontor i stan (in town). A company name needs no article: på Ikea. Arbetar means the same as jobbar; it is a little more formal.

Hemifrån (from home) and mestadels (mostly) are adverbs: they say where from and how much. På distans means remotely. To name your field, use inom: Jag jobbar inom IT. Not working at the moment? Say Jag studerar (or Jag pluggar, Lecture 3) or Jag söker jobb (I am looking for a job).

sections.title: Free time: what do you do?
body: The teacher’s homework question is Vad gör du på fritiden? (What do you do in your free time?). Answer with a verb in the present tense: Jag läser en bok. Jag lyssnar på musik. Jag tränar på gymmet.

English uses play for everything. Swedish has two verbs. Spelar is for games, sports and instruments: spelar datorspel, spelar fotboll, spelar piano. Leker is free play, the way children and pets play: leker med min katt.

Some free time is at home: stannar hemma (stay at home), vilar (rest), lagar mat (cook). Some is away: åker till havet (go to the sea), solar (sunbathe), badar (swim for fun), åker till fjällen (go to the mountains), åker skidor (ski), reser utomlands (travel abroad), går på bio (go to the cinema). Går en kurs means takes a course: en språkkurs, en matlagningskurs. In Finland, many people also bastar (take a sauna); you will hear går i bastu too.

Semester is a holiday from work (not a school term): Jag har semester or Jag är på semester. Fikar means having coffee and something sweet. Swedes say it all the time; in Finland, Swedish speakers usually say dricker kaffe.

examples.en: I play football and the piano.
examples.note: Spelar: a game, a sport or an instrument.

examples.en: I play with my cat.
examples.note: Leker: free play with a child or a pet.

examples.en: I am on holiday. I am going to the sea.
examples.note: Åker means going by car, bus, train or boat.

sections.title: Habits: brukar and time phrases
body: Brukar means usually: it says that something is a habit. It works like the help verbs in Lecture 3 (kan, vill, ska). Brukar is the present-tense verb, and the next verb stays in the infinitive (the basic form), with no att: brukar läsa, not brukar läser or brukar att läsa. Careful: brukar is not English used to, which is about the past. Jag brukar läsa means I usually read, now.

Word order works as in Lecture 3. A time phrase can come first; then the verb comes second and the subject after it: På helgen brukar jag läsa, not På helgen jag brukar läsa. Inte goes right after the first verb: Jag brukar inte träna. På helgen brukar jag inte träna.

Useful time phrases: på fritiden (in your free time), på helgen (at the weekend), på morgonen (in the morning), på eftermiddagen (in the afternoon), på kvällen (in the evening) and då och då (now and then, the same as ibland). Så fort som möjligt means as soon as possible.

Watch the small preposition before the time. På + kvällen, helgen, morgonen often describes a habit: på kvällen = in the evening, any evening. I + the time points to one particular time: i kväll = tonight, i helgen = this weekend. A trap: i morgon (Lecture 3) means tomorrow; in the morning is på morgonen. In Finland you will often hear på veckoslutet instead of på helgen; both are correct.

pronunciation.tip: Stress first, as in Lecture 1. Swedish-made words and compound words stress the first part: LÄ-rare, LÄ-kare, BOK-förare, DA-torspel, ÖN-skelista. Many job words are loanwords that stress the end, like ka-FÉ: ingen-JÖR, servi-TÖR, advo-KAT, program-ME-rare. In lärare and datorspel the Sweden-Swedish voices add a second, sing-song tone. Finland-Swedish has no such tone, so you do not need it: just stress the right syllable.

assignment.title: Episode 4 mission: My work and free time
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Say five lines: what you do, where you do it, how you work, and two free-time habits. Use brukar for at least one habit and a time phrase such as på helgen.

WRITE: Send your 25–45 word email to your new språkvän, with one question. Check that som + profession has no article.

RETURN: Tomorrow, say your work or study line and two habits without looking.
assignment.model: Jag jobbar som programmerare. Jag jobbar på ett företag i Helsingfors, men jag jobbar mestadels hemifrån. På helgen brukar jag läsa en bok. På kvällen lyssnar jag på musik. Då och då går jag på bio.

takeaways: Learn a noun with its article: en dator, ett jobb. Most nouns are en words, and endings help (-a, -ing, -are: en; -um: ett). The last part decides a compound word: ett datorspel.
Work: jobbar som + profession, with no article (not som en lärare); jobbar på + workplace, with its article.
Free time: spelar for games, sports and instruments; leker for free play with children and pets.
Habits: brukar + infinitive, with no att, like kan and vill. Put a time first and keep the verb second: På helgen brukar jag läsa. På helgen = every weekend; i helgen = this weekend.

Trött på says you have had enough of something: tired of.
Prova means try. Prova att vara: try being.

pages.intro: Maria and Nora use en and ett descriptions while talking about homes, jobs and a film. Watch the -t ending.

focus: bestämd form av substantiv: kafeet, livet, jobbet
recallCues: The narrator describes their small town, the small full café, what they talk about and Maria’s fun plan.

hunt.label: Ending hunt
hunt.title: Find the forms marked on the page
hunt.instructions: Tap each red or underlined word. Decide: an adjective for an en-word, an adjective for an ett-word, or a noun meaning “the”.

spots.rule: En liten stad: stad is an en-word, so liten keeps its basic form.
Ett litet kafe: liten becomes litet with an ett-word.
Kafeet means the café: ett kafe takes -et. Dictionary spelling: kaféet.
Kafeet är fullt: kafe is an ett-word, so full takes -t, even after är.
Livet means life: ett liv takes -et. Swedish uses the definite form for life in general.
Helgen means the weekend: en helg takes -en.
En rolig plan, en rolig film: en-words, so rolig has no -t.
Ett nytt hem, ett roligt nytt jobb: ny becomes nytt with an ett-word.
En ny lägenhet: lägenhet is an en-word, so ny has no -t.
Ett charmigt hus: charmig adds -t for an ett-word.
Landet: ett land takes -et. På landet means in the countryside.
Ett stort problem: stor adds -t for an ett-word.
Jobbet means the job: ett jobb takes -et. På jobbet means at work.
Chefen means the boss: en chef takes -en.
Chefen är sträng: chef is an en-word, so sträng has no -t.
Ett roligt nytt jobb: rolig adds -t because jobb is an ett-word.

sections.title: Say what you dream about
body: A dream can be a job, a home or something you want to learn. Use Jag drömmer om + a thing: Jag drömmer om ett hus. Use Jag vill bli + a job when you mean “I want to become”. After bli, a job has no en or ett: Jag vill bli fotograf.

Blir is the present tense of bli: När jag blir stor means when I grow up. Some words always bring the same small word with them, so learn them as chunks: intresserad av (interested in), ser upp till (look up to), trött på (tired of). English “interested in” tempts you to say intresserad i. Swedish always says intresserad av.
Byta jobb means change jobs; byta kläder means change clothes. The present tense is byter: Jag byter jobb. Går en kurs means takes or attends a course.

examples.fi: Jag drömmer om ett roligt jobb.
examples.en: I dream about a fun job.

examples.fi: Maja vill bli fotograf.
examples.en: Maja wants to become a photographer.

examples.fi: Alex är intresserad av fotografering.
examples.en: Alex is interested in photography.

examples.fi: Jag ser upp till min mamma.
examples.en: I look up to my mother.

examples.fi: Först går jag en kurs, och sedan byter jag jobb.
examples.en: First I take a course, and then I change jobs.

sections.memoryTip: Drömmer om points to the dream. Vill bli points to the person or job you want to become.
sections.tryIt: Finish aloud: Jag drömmer om … Jag är intresserad av … Jag vill …

activity.label: Dream builder
activity.title: Give each phrase its small word
activity.instructions: Each start needs its own small word: om, av, till or på. Match the pairs, then say each complete sentence.
activity.pattern: Learn the small word with the phrase: drömmer om, intresserad av, ser upp till, trött på. After bli, the job has no en or ett.

sections.title: Link one idea to the next
body: A conjunction is a small linking word. Och adds. Eller gives a choice. Men makes a contrast. Så gives a result. För gives a reason: here it means because.
After och, men, så and för, keep the normal order: the person, then the verb (så jag är trött). In writing, put a comma before men, så and för when a whole sentence follows.

Put the för part after the main idea: Jag kan inte träna, för jag är trött. English often starts with “Because …”, but Swedish för cannot start a sentence that way. Another word, eftersom, does that job later in the course.

Sedan (then) is a time adverb, not a conjunction. When it starts a sentence, the verb comes second, so the verb goes before the person: Sedan åker jag till jobbet. In speech, sedan is often shortened to sen. That is a spoken form.

examples.fi: Jag är intresserad av mode och smink.
examples.en: I am interested in fashion and make-up.

examples.fi: Vi kan dricka kaffe eller te.
examples.en: We can drink coffee or tea.

examples.fi: Jag vill träna, men jag hinner inte i dag.
examples.en: I want to exercise, but I do not have time today.

examples.fi: Jag pluggar svenska, så jag kan klara YKI-testet.
examples.en: I study Swedish, so I can pass the YKI test.

examples.fi: Jag kan inte sova, för jag dricker mycket kaffe.
examples.en: I cannot sleep because I drink a lot of coffee.

examples.fi: Jag äter frukost, och sedan åker jag till jobbet.
examples.en: I eat breakfast, and then I go to work.

sections.memoryTip: Reason → så → result. Result → för → reason. Your other languages help: för is like Hindi kyunki and Marathi karan (because); så is like Hindi isliye and Marathi mhanun (so).
sections.tryIt: Join aloud with men: Jag är trött. Jag vill prova. → Jag är trött, men jag vill prova.

activity.label: Join the ideas
activity.title: Which link makes sense?
activity.instructions: The linking word is missing. Read both ideas and choose the link that makes sense. Then say the whole sentence aloud with the link and a comma.

items.fi: Jag jobbar mycket … jag är trött.
items.en: I work a lot … I am tired.
items.why: Tired is the result of a lot of work: Jag jobbar mycket, så jag är trött.

items.fi: Jag är trött … jag jobbar mycket.
items.en: I am tired … I work a lot.
items.why: Now the reason comes second: Jag är trött, för jag jobbar mycket.

items.fi: Jag vill träna … jag hinner inte i dag.
items.en: I want to exercise … I do not have time today.
items.why: The second idea turns against the first: Jag vill träna, men jag hinner inte i dag.

items.fi: Vi kan dricka kaffe … te.
items.en: We can drink coffee … tea.
items.why: You choose one of two: kaffe eller te.

items.fi: Jag pluggar svenska … jag vill klara YKI-testet.
items.en: I study Swedish … I want to pass the YKI test.
items.why: Passing YKI is the reason you study: Jag pluggar svenska, för jag vill klara YKI-testet.

items.fi: Jag har ett prov snart … jag pluggar mycket.
items.en: I have a test soon … I study a lot.
items.why: Studying a lot is the result of the test: Jag har ett prov snart, så jag pluggar mycket.

items.fi: Jag gillar kaffe … te är bättre.
items.en: I like coffee … tea is better.
items.why: A contrast: Jag gillar kaffe, men te är bättre.

items.fi: Jag vill byta jobb … chefen är sträng.
items.en: I want to change jobs … the boss is strict.
items.why: The strict boss is the reason: Jag vill byta jobb, för chefen är sträng.

activity.summary: Ask: is the second idea the result (så) or the reason (för)? Swap the two ideas and så becomes för.

sections.title: Put “the” on the end
body: English puts the article “the” in front of a noun. Swedish usually adds it to the end of the noun instead. This is the definite form. An en-word adds -en or -n. An ett-word adds -et or -t. Hindi and Marathi have no word for “the” and often leave out “a”, so these small markers are easy to drop. Check every noun: en or ett, or the ending?

Learn each noun as a pair: en bok → boken, ett hus → huset. A word that already ends in a vowel adds only -n or -t: kvinna → kvinnan, äpple → äpplet. A few words that end in -el or -er also add only -n: en cykel → cykeln, en vinter → vintern.

When do you use it? Use en or ett the first time you mention something. Use the definite form when you both know which one you mean: Jag har en bil. Bilen är tysk. Some words are almost always definite: på jobbet (at work), i skolan (at school), livet (life) and världen (the world).

Mark “the” only once. Never use en and the ending together: boken, not en boken. After min or mitt (my) and after a name with -s, the noun stays bare, because those words already say whose it is: min bok, mitt kafé, Saras pappa (not min boken).

examples.fi: Jag har en bil. Bilen är tysk.
examples.en: I have a car. The car is German.

examples.fi: Jag har en snäll kollega på jobbet. Kollegan kommer från Sverige.
examples.en: I have a kind colleague at work. The colleague comes from Sweden.

examples.fi: På jobbet arbetar jag mycket.
examples.en: At work I work a lot.

examples.fi: I skolan läser vi svenska varje dag.
examples.en: At school we study Swedish every day.

examples.fi: Vi pratar om livet och världen.
examples.en: We talk about life and the world.

examples.fi: Min kamera är gammal, men bilden är fin.
examples.en: My camera is old, but the picture is nice.

sections.memoryTip: The small word en or ett moves to the back: en bok → bok-en; ett hus → hus-et. Once is enough: never en boken, never min boken.
sections.tryIt: Point to one thing near you and say three forms: en bok, boken, min bok.

activities.label: Ending sort
activities.title: Predict the ending for “the”
activities.instructions: Each card shows a noun with en or ett. Say the “the” form aloud first, then choose the ending you added.

items.fi: en bok
items.en: a book
items.why: En-word that ends in a consonant: en bok → boken.

items.fi: ett hus
items.en: a house
items.why: Ett-word that ends in a consonant: ett hus → huset.

items.fi: en kamera
items.en: a camera
items.why: En-word that already ends in a vowel: en kamera → kameran.

items.fi: ett äpple
items.en: an apple
items.why: Ett-word that already ends in a vowel: ett äpple → äpplet.

items.fi: ett jobb
items.en: a job
items.why: ett jobb → jobbet, as in på jobbet.

items.fi: en skola
items.en: a school
items.why: Ends in a vowel: en skola → skolan, as in i skolan.

items.fi: en värld
items.en: a world
items.why: en värld → världen.

items.fi: ett kafé
items.en: a café
items.why: An exception to the vowel clue: kafé ends in a stressed é, so it adds -et: kaféet, as on page 15.

activities.summary: En-word → -en or -n. Ett-word → -et or -t. Ending in a vowel → just -n or -t (but kaféet). Learn every noun with en or ett.

activities.label: Fix it
activities.title: Missing, one too many, or right?
activities.instructions: Each sentence should mean what the English says. Is en/ett or the ending missing, is there one too many, or is it right? Choose, then say the correct sentence aloud.

buckets.label: One too many
buckets.hint: Take away en/ett or the ending.

items.fi: Jag har bok.
items.en: I have a book.
items.why: A first mention needs en: Jag har en bok. Hindi and Marathi would say just “book” here, so en slips out easily.

items.fi: Min kameran är gammal.
items.en: My camera is old.
items.why: Min already says whose camera, so the noun stays bare: Min kamera är gammal.

items.fi: Jag har en bil. Bilen är tysk.
items.en: I have a car. The car is German.
items.why: First mention en bil, then bilen when you both know which car. Right.

items.fi: En boken är rolig.
items.en: The book is fun.
items.why: “The” goes on the end only: Boken är rolig. Never en and -en together.

items.fi: Kollega kommer från Sverige.
items.en: The colleague comes from Sweden.
items.why: “The colleague” needs the ending: Kollegan kommer från Sverige.

items.fi: Det är min syster.
items.en: That is my sister.
items.why: After min the noun stays bare: min syster, as in Lecture 2. Right.

items.fi: Saras pappan är fotograf.
items.en: Sara’s dad is a photographer.
items.why: A name with -s works like min: Saras pappa, with no ending, as on page 13.

items.fi: Han jobbar som en programmerare.
items.en: He works as a programmer.
items.why: No en with a job after som, as in Lecture 4: Han jobbar som programmerare.

items.fi: Jag pratar om livet.
items.en: I am talking about life.
items.why: English says just “life”, but Swedish uses the definite form for life in general: livet. Right.

activities.summary: Swedish marks “a” or “the” on almost every noun, but only once: en bok or boken, never en boken. After min, a name with -s, or jobbar som, the noun stays bare.

sections.title: Make the describing word fit
body: An adjective describes a noun: a fun film, a fun job. In Swedish the adjective changes to fit the noun’s group. This is called agreement. Use rolig with an en-word and roligt with an ett-word.

Most adjectives just add -t for an ett-word: rolig → roligt, stor → stort, gammal → gammalt, vacker → vackert. Two common ones change more: ny → nytt (double t) and liten → litet. Adjectives that already end in -tt stay the same: ett lätt jobb, ett trött barn. A few never change, such as bra: en bra film, ett bra jobb.

The same ending comes after är: Boken är rolig. Huset är stort. Kaféet är fullt. After det är, use the -t form too: Det är roligt! Det är inte lätt. The usual slip is a missing -t: ett rolig jobb, det är rolig. These forms are for one thing (singular); plural forms come later.
Lite (a little) is a different word. It is an adverb: it tells how much, and it never changes. Jag pratar lite svenska. Never say liten svenska.

examples.fi: Jag läser en rolig bok.
examples.en: I am reading a fun book.

examples.fi: Jag har ett roligt jobb.
examples.en: I have a fun job.

examples.fi: Vi bor i ett litet hus.
examples.en: We live in a small house.

examples.fi: Huset är stort.
examples.en: The house is big.

examples.fi: Det är inte lätt, men det är roligt.
examples.en: It is not easy, but it is fun.

examples.fi: Jag pratar lite svenska.
examples.en: I speak a little Swedish.

sections.memoryTip: Hear ett, expect a -t sound on the adjective too: ett roligt jobb.
sections.tryIt: Say the pairs aloud: rolig film, roligt jobb; stor lägenhet, stort hus; liten paus, litet barn.

activity.label: En or ett?
activity.title: Read the adjective, find the noun’s group
activity.instructions: The small word en or ett is hidden. Look at the adjective’s ending and decide which group the noun belongs to. Then say the phrase with en or ett.

buckets.label: en-word
buckets.hint: The adjective has its basic form: rolig, liten, gammal.

buckets.label: ett-word
buckets.hint: The adjective has its -t form: roligt, nytt, litet.

items.fi: rolig bok
items.en: fun book
items.why: No -t on rolig, so bok is an en-word: en rolig bok.

items.fi: roligt jobb
items.en: fun job
items.why: Roligt has -t, so jobb is an ett-word: ett roligt jobb.

items.fi: tråkigt möte
items.en: boring meeting
items.why: Tråkigt has -t: ett tråkigt möte.

items.fi: farlig hund
items.en: dangerous dog
items.why: No -t on farlig: en farlig hund.

items.fi: nytt kafé
items.en: new café
items.why: Ny becomes nytt with an ett-word: ett nytt kafé.

items.fi: liten paus
items.en: small break
items.why: Liten is the en form: en liten paus.

items.fi: litet barn
items.en: small child
items.why: Liten becomes litet with an ett-word: ett litet barn.

items.fi: gammal vän
items.en: old friend
items.why: No -t on gammal: en gammal vän.

activity.summary: The noun’s group controls the adjective. Learn en or ett with every new noun.

guided.prompt: Produce: “I dream about a fun job.”
answers: Jag drömmer om ett roligt jobb.
Jag drömmer om ett kul jobb.
Jag drömmer om ett roligt arbete.
Jag drömmer om ett kul arbete.
guided.hint: Use drömmer om. Jobb is an ett-word.
guided.explanation: Jag drömmer om ett roligt jobb: you met ett jobb in Lecture 4, so rolig takes -t. Kul never changes, so ett kul jobb is right too.

guided.prompt: Jag vill byta jobb, ___ chefen är sträng.
guided.hint: The second idea gives the reason.
guided.explanation: För means because here.

guided.prompt: Jag har en bok. ___ är rolig.
guided.hint: Now you mean the book already introduced.
guided.explanation: En bok becomes boken in the definite form.

guided.prompt: Produce: “a charming house in the countryside”.
guided.hint: Hus is an ett-word, so charmig takes -t. In the countryside: på landet.
guided.explanation: Ett charmigt hus på landet: the adjective adds -t before the ett-word hus, as on page 15.

guided.prompt: Fix it: “För jag är trött, jag kan inte träna.” (It should mean: I can’t exercise because I am tired.)
answers: Jag kan inte träna, för jag är trött.
Jag är trött, så jag kan inte träna.
guided.hint: För cannot open the sentence. Put the main idea first. Inte goes straight after kan.
guided.explanation: Jag kan inte träna, för jag är trött: the för part comes second, and inte follows the first verb kan, as in Lecture 3. Turning it round with så also works: Jag är trött, så jag kan inte träna.

guided.prompt: Var är ___? Jag måste ringa Elin. (You mean your own phone.)
guided.hint: You both know which phone you mean.
guided.explanation: Use the definite form for a thing you both know: Var är mobilen?

guided.prompt: Produce: “The house is not big.”
guided.hint: The house: the definite form of ett hus. Inte goes straight after är (Lecture 3).
guided.explanation: Huset är inte stort: huset means the house, inte follows the verb är as in Lecture 3, and stort keeps the -t because hus is an ett-word.

guided.prompt: Produce: “It is fun!” (Start with Det är …)
guided.hint: After det är, the adjective takes its -t form.
guided.explanation: Det är roligt: det works like an ett-word, so rolig takes -t. Kul and skoj never change, so Det är kul! is also right.

guided.prompt: Produce: “I speak a little Swedish.”
guided.hint: Use the amount word lite, not the adjective liten. Pratar, talar or kan all work.
guided.explanation: Lite describes the amount, as in your Lecture 1 introduction: Jag talar hindi och lite svenska. Liten would describe a small noun.

guided.prompt: Build the next step: “First I take a course, and then I apply for a job.”
answers: Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag jobb.
Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag ett jobb.
Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag arbete.
Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag ett arbete.
Först går jag en kurs, och sen söker jag jobb.
Först går jag en kurs, och sen söker jag ett jobb.
Först går jag en kurs, och sen söker jag arbete.
Först går jag en kurs, och sen söker jag ett arbete.

guided.hint: After the opening time word, the verb comes before jag.

Arbetet är tråkigt, så jag vill ha ett nytt jobb.
checkpoint.hint: Start with “the job” (definite form). Jobb is an ett-word, so both adjectives take -t. Link with så.

checkpoint.prompt: Which phrase is correct?

checkpoint.explanation: Ett kafé needs litet. Lite means a little (an amount), so ett lite kafé is wrong.

assignment.title: Episode 5 mission: My dream
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Tell Elin your dream in five or six linked sentences. Say what you dream about, what interests you, what you want to do, why, one difficulty, and one next step. Use men, så and för.

WRITING: Reply to Elin’s message Vad drömmer du om? Give your dream, a reason with för and your first step, then ask her back: Och du?

RETURN: Tomorrow, say your dream and reason from memory in under 30 seconds.
assignment.model: Jag drömmer om ett roligt jobb. Jag är intresserad av språk och fotografering, så jag vill göra något kreativt. Jag vill byta jobb, för jag vill lära mig något nytt. Det är inte lätt, men jag vill prova. Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag ett nytt jobb.

takeaways: Link ideas: och adds, eller offers a choice, men contrasts, så gives a result, för gives a reason (never at the start of the sentence), and sedan moves to the next action.
Put “the” on the noun: en bok → boken, ett hus → huset, en kvinna → kvinnan, ett äpple → äpplet. Mark it only once: boken and min bok, never en boken or min boken.
Let the adjective follow en or ett: en rolig film but ett roligt jobb; ny → nytt and liten → litet; after det är: Det är roligt. Lite (a little) never changes.

pronunciation.text: En rolig film. Ett roligt jobb. En stor lägenhet. Ett stort hus. En ny mobil. Ett nytt kafé. En liten paus. Ett litet barn. Boken, huset, kvinnan, äpplet.
pronunciation.tip: The -t carries the grammar: ett roligt jobb, ett stort hus. Make it clear, with the tongue tip forward at or just behind the top teeth (like Hindi त, not ट; Indian English often curls t back). In roligt the g is silent: “rolit”. Ny has a long y; nytt has a short y and a long t. Then contrast liten, litet and lite. Finland-Swedish note: the Sweden-Swedish voices merge r + t in stort into one curled-back sound, close to ट; in Finland you say r and t separately: stor-t.

spots.rule: Past, group 1: klarar → klarade.
Past, group 1: pluggar → pluggade.
Past, group 1: pratar → pratade.
Direction: Sofia moves toward home (kommer hem).
Location: the party is at home (en fest hemma).
Ett prov: prov is an ett-word.
Ett prov = a test, not a known one yet.
Definite form: ett prov → provet, the test.
En fest: fest is an en-word.
En fest = a party, not a known one yet.
Definite form: en fest → festen, the party.

pages.title: Textbook page practice: Hur var det på festen?
pages.tabLabel: Page 17 · Hur var det på festen?

lines.speaker: Berättare
lines.fi: Sara kom till Sofias hus igår. Hon köpte en present till Sofia. Det var en bok som de tittade på förra veckan. Sofia ville ha boken men hon hade inte några pengar. Därför blev Sofia mycket glad när hon såg boken. Hennes favoritförfattare skrev den.
lines.en: Sara came to Sofia’s house yesterday. She bought a present for Sofia. It was a book they looked at last week. Sofia wanted the book, but she didn’t have any money. So Sofia was very happy when she saw the book. Her favourite author wrote it.

lines.fi: På festen spelade de mycket bra musik och dansade. Sofias granne klagade på musiken men de gav henne lite tårta så hon lämnade. Lite senare åt de en fin middag. Sara gick hem klockan 8. Hon sa att hon måste vakna tidigt. Efter festen läste Sofia boken.
lines.en: At the party they played very good music and danced. Sofia’s neighbour complained about the music, but they gave her some cake, so she left. A little later they ate a nice dinner. Sara went home at eight. She said that she had to wake up early. After the party Sofia read the book.

naturalNotes.note: Lämna normally needs an object: hon lämnade festen (she left the party). Hon lämnade on its own copies English “she left” and sounds new to many Swedish speakers. Say hon gick därifrån (she went away from there) or hon gick hem.

homework.title: Diary
homework.instructions: Skriv dagbok varje dag, 5–10 minuter. Write a few lines about your day in the past tense, especially with irregular verbs (åt, drack, gick, såg). After a time word the verb comes second: Igår vaknade jag tidigt.
homework.note: This is a recurring task with no due date: write a new short entry every day. There is no answer key; check your entry against the points and the model.

questions.prompt: Skriv om ditt vardagsliv. Vad gjorde du igår? Använd preteritum, särskilt oregelbundna verb. Skriv om dig själv, dina vanor, vad du gillar och inte gillar och om människor i ditt liv.
questions.translation: Write about your daily life. What did you do yesterday? Use the past tense, especially irregular verbs. Write about yourself, your habits, your likes and dislikes, and the people in your life.

points: I wrote what I did, in the past tense (preteritum).
I used at least three irregular verbs (for example åt, drack, gick, såg, fick, var, hade).
I used time words (igår, imorse, förra veckan) and put the verb second after them: Igår vaknade jag…
I said something I like or do not like.
I wrote about a person in my life (a friend, a colleague, my family).

sections.title: Build regular past forms
body: Past tense tells what happened at a finished time: igår (yesterday), igår kväll (yesterday evening), i lördags (last Saturday: i + day + s), förra veckan (last week), förra året (last year). For “ago”, put the time between för and sedan: för fem år sedan = five years ago. Sedan on its own means then: Sedan gick jag hem.
With a finished time such as igår or för … sedan, Swedish uses this past form. Indian English often says I have come here two years back; in Swedish say Jag kom hit för två år sedan.
The past form is the same for every person: jag jobbade, du jobbade, hon jobbade, vi jobbade. Unlike Hindi (gaya, gayi, gaye) or English (was, were), it never changes for a man, a woman or a group.
Your teacher’s clue: look at the present tense form. Verbs with -ar in the present are group 1. Keep the -a of the base form and add -de: jobbar → jobba → jobbade, dansar → dansade.

Most group 2 verbs have -er in the present. Take away -er and add -de: ringer → ringde, beställer → beställde. If what is left ends in p, k, t, s or x, add -te instead: köper → köpte, tycker → tyckte, läser → läste. These sounds are voiceless: your throat does not buzz when you say them. The -te rule is only for -er verbs; pratar is group 1, so it becomes pratade.

Group 3 verbs are short and end in a vowel + r in the present: bor, mår, tror. They add -dde: bodde, mådde, trodde. Careful: some of the most common verbs break these patterns (har → hade, tar → tog, går → gick, äter → åt). Learn those as pairs in the next topic.

When a time word comes first, the verb still comes second and jag moves after it: Igår jobbade jag. Not: Igår jag jobbade. This is the verb-second word order from Lecture 3. Learners of every language find it hard, so practise it with every time word in your story: Sedan åkte jag …, På kvällen åt jag …

activity.summary: Read the present form first: -ar → -ade; -er → -de, or -te after p, k, t, s, x; short verbs with a vowel + r → -dde. Very common verbs such as går, äter and har are irregular: learn them as pairs.

sections.title: Learn the common irregular pairs
body: Some very common verbs do not follow the regular patterns. Often the vowel inside the verb changes (dricker → drack, skriver → skrev); sometimes the whole word changes (är → var). Learn each present–past pair as one chunk, and never add -de to them: sov, not sovde. Careful: går looks like mår (mådde), but går → gick. The textbook calls them starka verb (strong verbs); this course calls them irregular verbs.

Start with the forms you need to tell a whole day: är → var, har → hade, går → gick, äter → åt, dricker → drack, sover → sov, gör → gjorde, kommer → kom. Page 18 has ten more. Learn a few each day in your diary.

The help verbs from Lecture 3 have past forms too: kan → kunde, vill → ville, and måste stays måste. The next verb stays in its base form, and inte still comes right after the first verb: Jag kunde inte komma. Sofia ville ha boken.
A trap: var can mean was (Jag var hemma) or where (Var bor du?), so Var var du? means Where were you?

Swedish has no did. In a yes/no question the past verb simply comes first: Åt du frukost? (Did you eat breakfast?) Hade du en bra dag på jobbet? (Did you have a good day at work?) In a negative sentence inte comes after the past verb: Jag sov inte bra. (I did not sleep well.) Never use gjorde for did: Åt du? (not Gjorde du äta?)

sections.title: React to good news
body: A story about the past is also a conversation. When a friend tells you news, react first, then ask one follow-up question.

Big good news: Vilka fantastiska nyheter! (What fantastic news!) or Grattis! (Congratulations!). Nyheter is plural in Swedish (en nyhet = one piece of news), so you say vilka, not vilken. Smaller good news: Vad roligt! (How nice!) or Vad bra! (How good!). Bad news: Vad tråkigt! (What a pity!). Tråkig also means boring, but as a reaction it means I am sorry to hear that. Surprise: Oj! (Oh!). Jag är stolt över dig means I am proud of you.
Then ask a past question: Hur var det? (How was it?) or Vad gjorde du? (What did you do?).

sections.title: Go home, then be at home
body: Hem shows direction: you move toward home. Hemma shows location: you are already there. English says “home” for both, so look at the verb.

Movement verbs take hem: gå hem (go home on foot), åka hem (go home by bus, tram or car), komma hem. Being or doing something there takes hemma: Jag var hemma. Jag jobbade hemma. Hemma åt jag middag. Careful: English went covers both gick and åkte. Gick means you walked; by tram, bus or train say åkte (åker → åkte is regular: -te after k).
The same idea works for ut–ute (out–outside), in–inne (in–inside), upp–uppe (up–upstairs) and ner–nere (down–downstairs). The short form shows movement; the form ending in -a or -e shows location.
Two useful chunks: hem till mig (to my place) and hemma hos mig (at my place).

pronunciation.text: jobbade, pratade, vaknade, köpte. Gick, gjorde. Jag gick hem. Jag var hemma.
pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the ending light but audible: JOBbade, PRAtade, VAKnade, KÖPte. The Sweden-Swedish voices give these words a falling-then-rising tune (accent 2). Standard Finland-Swedish has no such tune, only plain stress, so you do not need it. In relaxed speech many Swedes clip -ade to -a (jag jobba igår): recognise it, but write -ade. Gick and gjorde start with an English y sound (Lecture 1). Hem has one syllable, hemma two.

assignment.title: Episode 6 mission: Yesterday
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Tell your day yesterday in six lines, from morning to evening, as in the YKI telling task. Use at least four past verbs.

WRITING: Write to a friend whose party you missed: say sorry, say why, tell one thing you did and ask how it was.

DAILY: Start your diary today and write for 5–10 minutes every day, as your teacher asked. Each day, use at least two irregular past forms and one new word about your own life.

assignment.model: Igår vaknade jag klockan sju och åt frukost. Sedan åkte jag till jobbet med spårvagnen. På jobbet pratade jag med en kollega. Efter jobbet köpte jag mat och åkte hem. Hemma åt jag middag och pluggade svenska. Dagen var lång men bra.

takeaways: Use one past form for every person: jag jobbade, hon jobbade, vi jobbade.
Read the present form: -ar → -ade, -er → -de (or -te after p, k, t, s, x), short verbs with a vowel + r → -dde.
Learn frequent irregular verbs as pairs, with no ending: är–var, går–gick, äter–åt, sover–sov, kan–kunde.
After a time word the verb comes second (Igår gick jag hem), and Swedish has no did (Åt du? Jag åt inte).
Hem is a direction; hemma is a location. React to news before asking what happened.

homework.title: Noun plurals

sections.title: Meet the five plural groups
body: Plural means two or more. English usually adds -s: one car, two cars. Swedish has five plural endings, so your teacher sorts nouns into five plural groups.
Two clues point to the group. Is the noun an en-word or an ett-word? And what is its last letter? En blomma is an en-word that ends in -a, so it is group 1: två blommor.
These are the teacher's clues, not laws. They work for many nouns, and the teacher lists the exceptions you need now. Learn every new noun as a pair: en bil, två bilar.
To count, put the number before the plural. One is en or ett, so it matches the noun: en bil, ett äpple. From two upwards, use the plural: två bilar, tre äpplen.

Two mistakes cost the most. Do not give every noun the same ending, as English does with -s: två vänner and två hus, not två vännar or två husar. And do not drop the ending after a number: två bilar, not två bil.

short everyday en-word; e as the last or second-last letter; ends in -ing
hund → hundar, pojke → pojkar, cykel → cyklar, klänning → klänningar
banan → bananer, tomat → tomater, frisör → frisörer, ingenjör → ingenjörer
äpple → äpplen, konto → konton, meddelande → meddelanden

sections.memoryTip: Hindi and Marathi also change the end of a noun in the plural: लड़का → लड़के, मुलगा → मुलगे. Many Hindi and Marathi nouns keep the same form in the plural (Hindi एक घर, दो घर), just like Swedish group 5: ett hus, två hus. In Swedish only group 5 works like that, so two cars is två bilar, never två bil.

sections.title: Groups 1 and 2: -or and -ar
body: Group 1: en-words that end in -a. Take away the -a and add -or: en blomma → blommor, en vecka → veckor, en kvinna → kvinnor, en flaska → flaskor.
Group 2 takes -ar. The teacher gives three clues. First, many short everyday en-words: en bil → bilar, en hund → hundar, en buss → bussar.

Second, en-words with e as the last or second-last letter. That e drops before -ar: en pojke → pojkar, en cykel → cyklar. Third, words that end in -ing: en tidning → tidningar, en klänning → klänningar.
The short-word clue is the weakest. Sak, katt, chef and vän look like group 2, but they take -er, and so does gäst (guest) from the dialogue. You meet them in the next topic.

sections.title: Group 3 and the teacher's exceptions
body: Group 3 takes -er. The teacher's clue: words that came into Swedish from other languages (loanwords). En banan → bananer, en tomat → tomater, en apelsin → apelsiner, and job words on -ör: en frisör → frisörer, en servitör → servitörer, en ingenjör → ingenjörer, en direktör → direktörer.

You cannot always know where a word comes from, so listen to it. Many group 3 loanwords are stressed on the last syllable: ba-NAN, to-MAT, apel-SIN, fri-SÖR, bil-JETT, tele-FON. Stress at the end is a strong hint for -er.
Two ett-words also take -er: ett museum → museer (take away -um first) and ett protein → proteiner. Ett vitamin → vitaminer on page 23 works the same way.

Four short en-words look like group 2 but take -er: en sak → saker, en katt → katter, en chef → chefer, en vän → vänner. En gäst → gäster from the dialogue works the same way. The ä in vän is short, so the n is written twice when an ending follows: vänner.
A few -er words also change their vowel: en bok → böcker, en son → söner (page 23). Learn these exceptions as whole pairs. Do not build a new rule from them.

sections.title: Groups 4 and 5: ett-words and jobs on -are
body: Group 4: ett-words that end in a vowel. Just add -n: ett möte → möten, ett äpple → äpplen, ett konto → konton, ett meddelande → meddelanden.
This -n is not the definite form from Lecture 5, where the ending means the: äpplet = the apple, but äpplen = apples; mötet = the meeting, but möten = meetings.

Group 5: ett-words that end in a consonant. Add nothing: ett jobb → två jobb, ett företag → två företag, ett barn → två barn, ett hus → två hus. The number or a word like många shows that it is plural.

Group 5 also has some en-words for jobs and origins. The teacher's examples end in -are: en lärare → två lärare, en läkare → två läkare, en italienare → två italienare. Here in Finland: en finländare → två finländare. Job words on -ör, like frisör, stay in group 3.

sections.title: Choose många or mycket
body: Use många (many) with plural things you count one by one: många bilar, många möten. Ask Hur många …? and answer with a number: Hur många bilar har ni? – Två.
Use mycket (much, a lot of) with an amount you do not count piece by piece: mycket vin, mycket kaffe, mycket tid. Ask Hur mycket …?
Pengar (money) is a plural word, but Swedish still says mycket pengar, because money is an amount. A container makes an amount countable: två flaskor vatten, tre koppar kaffe.

English a lot of fits both, and so do Hindi बहुत and Marathi खूप. Swedish makes you choose: a lot of cars is många bilar, never mycket bilar. The small words work the same way: några (some, a few) before plurals, lite (a little) before an amount: några tomater, lite mjölk.
Mycket also goes with verbs: Jag jobbar mycket (I work a lot). And inga means no before a plural: Jag har inga katter.

examples.fi: Jag har många böcker hemma.
examples.en: I have many books at home.

examples.fi: Hur mycket kaffe dricker du?

examples.en: They want to earn a lot of money.

sections.memoryTip: If a number fits in front, use många: tre böcker → många böcker. If no number fits, as with pengar, tid or kaffe, use mycket. A lot of cars = många bilar.

sections.title: Meet, see and play: verb pairs
body: Träffar means meet someone. A person comes after it (the object): Jag träffar Elin i kväll. Träffas means meet each other, so no person comes after it: Vi träffas i kväll. In the past: träffade and träffades.
Ser and ses work the same way: Vi ser en älg (we see a moose). Vi ses! means See you! (we will see each other).
Swedish has two verbs for play. Leker is play for children and pets: Barnen leker i trädgården. Spelar is for games, sports and instruments: Jag spelar fotboll. Alex spelar datorspel.
Lagar means repair: Han lagar cyklar. Laga mat means cook: Vi lagar mat tillsammans.

examples.fi: Jag träffar Elin i kväll.
examples.en: I am meeting Elin tonight.

examples.fi: Vi träffas i kväll.
examples.en: We are meeting (each other) tonight.

assignment.title: Episode 7 mission: Things at home
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Answer the YKI-style interview theme Berätta om ditt hem (Tell about your home) in five or six sentences. Use at least three plural groups, one exact number, många, mycket and inga, and link two ideas with men or för.

WRITING: Answer a friend at the shop with a short shopping message (30–55 words).

RETURN: Tomorrow, name five things at home from memory and give their plurals.
assignment.model: Hemma har jag två lampor, fyra stolar, många böcker, fem blommor och två cyklar.

takeaways: Group 1 (-or): en-words ending in -a, en blomma → blommor. Group 2 (-ar): many short en-words, and words with e near the end or -ing, en pojke → pojkar.

Group 3 (-er): words from other languages, often stressed on the last syllable (bananer, telefoner), plus the exceptions saker, katter, chefer, vänner, gäster, museer, proteiner. Group 4 (-n): ett-words ending in a vowel; äpplen = apples, but äpplet = the apple. Group 5 (no ending): ett-words ending in a consonant, and jobs on -are.

Count with många and några; describe an amount with mycket and lite. Avoid the three big mistakes: två bil, två vännar, mycket bilar. You träffar someone, but vi träffas; children leker, and you spelar games.

pronunciation.text: En blomma, två blommor. En bil, två bilar. En banan, två bananer. Ett museum, två museer. Ett möte, två möten. En vän, två vänner.
pronunciation.tip: The stress stays on the same syllable as in the singular: BI-lar, ba-NA-ner, mu-SE-er (say both e's). Say the unstressed ending clearly, because it is the only sign of the group. Finland-Swedish weakens endings less than the Sweden-Swedish voices do, and it has no two-step word melody (accent 2) on words like bilar and blommor, so you do not need to copy that melody. Keep the ä short in vän and vänner.

listening.text: Elin och Mikko bor i en lägenhet med tre rum. I vardagsrummet har de en soffa, fyra stolar och många böcker. På bordet står två lampor och tre glas. De har också fem blommor men inga katter. I köket finns många tallrikar, några flaskor vatten och sex äpplen. Elin dricker mycket kaffe, så hon har många koppar. Två dagar i veckan jobbar hon hemma. Då har hon många videomöten. Hon tycker om museer och har två biljetter till Ateneum på söndag.
